In many real-life machine learning applications, the uncertainty of the inputs is negligible. Image classifiers, for example, often see photographs with a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), the measured signal divided by its uncertainty, above 100 or even 1000. The input uncertainty then plays almost no role in the inference.

In astronomy, the situation is often different. Both the inputs \(x\) and the outputs \(y\) can carry large uncertainties. Astronomical images and spectra often have an SNR near 10, and sometimes near 1. The input uncertainty can then reach 10% or even 100% of the signal. Derived quantities, such as the black hole masses and velocity dispersions of the M-\(\sigma\) relation, can have large uncertainties as well. These uncertainties often reach about 10% of the full range of the observed values.

Chapters 4 and 5 ignored the input uncertainties. When we ignore them, the estimated slope is biased toward zero, which weakens (attenuates) the relation. This effect is called attenuation bias, or regression dilution. Statisticians have studied it at length under the names measurement error models and errors-in-variables regression, that is, regression with uncertain inputs. It also arises in other machine learning models with uncertain inputs. Linear regression is a good place to study it, because the algebra is exact and the geometry is clear.

We first build intuition for why input uncertainty weakens the relation, then derive the bias and see how large it is in astronomy. We start with equal uncertainties for all points and let them differ at the end. Next we treat the true \(x\)-values as hidden, or latent, variables and infer them together with the model parameters. This leads to Deming regression, which accounts for uncertainties in both variables and corrects the underestimate of the slope that ordinary least squares (OLS) gives. The method is linear, but what we learn about handling input uncertainties applies broadly across statistical inference in astronomy.

6.1 Attenuation Bias

Consider a linear relation between \(y\) and \(x\), such as the M-\(\sigma\) relation. If we measured \(x\) perfectly but had uncertainties in \(y\), the data would scatter vertically around the true relation, as in Figure 6.1(a). As in the previous chapters, maximum likelihood or Bayesian methods can recover the true relation when they account for these \(y\)-uncertainties.

Now suppose that \(x\) is uncertain too. Each point then scatters both horizontally and vertically from its true position, as in panel (b). The horizontal scatter inflates the range of \(x\), the interval between its smallest and largest values, as the bands in Figure 6.1 show. The range along \(y\) has no matching increase.

Let \(\sigma_x\) be the standard deviation of the \(x\)-errors and \(\sigma_{\text{range}}\) the standard deviation of the true \(x\)-values. For a small error, such as \(\sigma_x/\sigma_{\text{range}} = 0.1\), the observed range grows only modestly. For \(\sigma_x/\sigma_{\text{range}} = 1\), as in panel (b), the inflation is large.

In the extreme case, the \(x\)-uncertainty grows without limit and the \(x\)-measurements become pure noise with no correlation to their true values. Any relation is then hidden, and the fitted line becomes horizontal.

Why does the vertical scatter not cause the same problem? In regression, \(x\) and \(y\) play different roles. A fit asks what \(y\)-value to expect for a given \(x\)-value. Uncertainty in \(y\) adds noise to this prediction, which averages out with enough data. Uncertainty in \(x\) changes the question. We now predict \(y\) from a noisy version of \(x\), which flattens the relation that we find.

6.2 Mathematical Model

To make this intuition precise, we need a model of the true relation and of the measurement errors. We take the simplest case first, univariate (one input variable) linear regression with homogeneous, or homoscedastic, uncertainties. This case is restrictive, but its analytical results show how attenuation bias arises. Section 6.8 treats the heteroscedastic case, in which the uncertainties differ from point to point.

The true relation that we want to measure is \[ y_{\text{true}} = \gamma x_{\text{true}}, \] where \(\gamma\) is the true slope. In the M-\(\sigma\) relation, \(x_{\text{true}}\) is the logarithm of the true velocity dispersion and \(y_{\text{true}}\) is the logarithm of the true black hole mass.

We do not measure these true values directly. The measurements contain errors \[\begin{aligned} x_{\text{obs}} &= x_{\text{true}} + \delta_x \\ y_{\text{obs}} &= y_{\text{true}} + \delta_y = \gamma x_{\text{true}} + \delta_y. \end{aligned}\]

To analyze this model, we make three assumptions about the errors.

First, the errors are unbiased \[\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}[\delta_x] &= 0 \\ \mathbb{E}[\delta_y] &= 0. \end{aligned}\] This means that our measurements do not systematically over- or underestimate the true values. In astronomy, we calibrate our instruments and correct for known systematic effects to ensure this property.

Second, the errors have homogeneous variances \[\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(\delta_x) &= \sigma_x^2 \\ \text{Var}(\delta_y) &= \sigma_y^2. \end{aligned}\] These variances do not change from point to point.

Third, the errors are independent of the true values and of each other. This is often approximately true in astronomy. Photon noise in different measurements, for example, is typically independent. Instrumental effects usually do not depend on the signal that we measure.

It is also useful to work with centered variables, which are shifted to have zero mean. For the inputs, centering puts the pivot of Section 5.5 at the mean of the \(x\)-values, which makes the intercept and the slope uncorrelated. We redefine the observed variables by subtracting their means \[\begin{aligned} x_{\text{obs}} &\leftarrow x_{\text{obs}} - \mathbb{E}[x_{\text{obs}}] \\ y_{\text{obs}} &\leftarrow y_{\text{obs}} - \mathbb{E}[y_{\text{obs}}]. \end{aligned}\]Centered variables simplify the algebra and focus attention on how changes in \(x\) relate to changes in \(y\).

6.3 Maximum Likelihood with Input Uncertainties

We now connect this model to maximum likelihood estimation. In Chapter 4 we showed that, for homogeneous noise, the maximum likelihood estimator has a matrix form. Here both variables have observed and true values. We therefore write the observed outputs, called \(\mathbf{t}\) there, as \(\mathbf{y}_{\text{obs}}\), like \(x_{\text{obs}}\). The estimator reads \[ \mathbf{w}_{\text{ML}} = (\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\boldsymbol{\Phi})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{y}_{\text{obs}}. \]

Simple linear regression with one input variable is a special case of this formula. Because the variables are centered, the intercept is zero and we estimate only the slope. The design matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}\) is then a vector of the \(N\) observed \(x\)-values \[ \boldsymbol{\Phi} = \begin{bmatrix} x_{\text{obs},1} & x_{\text{obs},2} & \cdots & x_{\text{obs},N} \end{bmatrix}^T. \]The two matrix products reduce to sums \[\begin{aligned} \boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\boldsymbol{\Phi} &= \begin{bmatrix} x_{\text{obs},1} & x_{\text{obs},2} & \cdots & x_{\text{obs},N} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_{\text{obs},1} \\ x_{\text{obs},2} \\ \vdots \\ x_{\text{obs},N} \end{bmatrix} = \sum_{i=1}^N x_{\text{obs},i}^2 \\ \boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{y}_{\text{obs}} &= \begin{bmatrix} x_{\text{obs},1} & x_{\text{obs},2} & \cdots & x_{\text{obs},N} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} y_{\text{obs},1} \\ y_{\text{obs},2} \\ \vdots \\ y_{\text{obs},N} \end{bmatrix} = \sum_{i=1}^N x_{\text{obs},i}y_{\text{obs},i}. \end{aligned}\]The matrix equation then reduces to the scalar OLS slope estimate \(\hat{\gamma}\), where the hat distinguishes the estimate from the true slope \(\gamma\) \[ \hat{\gamma} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^N x_{\text{obs},i}y_{\text{obs},i}}{\sum_{i=1}^N x_{\text{obs},i}^2}. \]

We can also write this solution as a ratio of a covariance to a variance \[ \hat{\gamma} = \frac{\text{Cov}(x_{\text{obs}}, y_{\text{obs}})}{\text{Var}(x_{\text{obs}})}. \]In this form, the numerator measures how much \(y\) changes as \(x\) varies. The denominator measures the spread of the \(x\)-values. Their ratio is the change in \(y\) per unit change in \(x\), the slope. This interpretation holds only if the denominator is the variance of the true \(x\)-values.

To see how the uncertainties affect the estimate, we analyze the numerator and the denominator separately. For a large sample, the sample covariance and variance approach their expectations, which we compute. We start with the numerator, the covariance of the observed quantities. We use the expressions for the centered variables and the linearity of the covariance. Linearity means that \(\text{Cov}(X + Y, Z) = \text{Cov}(X, Z) + \text{Cov}(Y, Z)\) for random variables \(X\), \(Y\) and \(Z\), and that constant factors come out of either argument \[\begin{aligned} \text{Cov}(x_{\text{obs}}, y_{\text{obs}}) &= \text{Cov}(x_{\text{true}} + \delta_x, \gamma x_{\text{true}} + \delta_y) \\ &= \gamma \text{Cov}(x_{\text{true}} + \delta_x, x_{\text{true}}) + \text{Cov}(x_{\text{true}} + \delta_x, \delta_y) \\ &= \gamma [\text{Cov}(x_{\text{true}}, x_{\text{true}}) + \text{Cov}(\delta_x, x_{\text{true}})] + [\text{Cov}(x_{\text{true}}, \delta_y) + \text{Cov}(\delta_x, \delta_y)] \\ &= \gamma [\text{Var}(x_{\text{true}}) + 0] + [0 + 0] \\ &= \gamma \text{Var}(x_{\text{true}}). \end{aligned}\]

The expansion in the third line has four contributions. The first, \(\text{Cov}(x_{\text{true}}, x_{\text{true}})\), is the spread of the true values, which is \(\text{Var}(x_{\text{true}})\). The second, \(\text{Cov}(\delta_x, x_{\text{true}})\), links the measurement errors to the true values. The third, \(\text{Cov}(x_{\text{true}}, \delta_y)\), links the \(y\)-errors to the true \(x\)-values. The fourth, \(\text{Cov}(\delta_x, \delta_y)\), links the \(x\)-errors to the \(y\)-errors.

Our independence assumptions make the last three terms zero, because measurement errors do not depend on the true values or on each other. Independent variables have zero covariance (Section 3.6). Therefore \[ \text{Cov}(x_{\text{obs}}, y_{\text{obs}}) = \gamma \text{Var}(x_{\text{true}}) \equiv \gamma \sigma_{\text{range}}^2. \] Here \(\sigma_{\text{range}}^2\) is the variance of the true \(x\)-values, so \(\sigma_{\text{range}}\) is their standard deviation. In the M-\(\sigma\) relation, it is the spread of the true velocity dispersions of the galaxies in the sample.

For the denominator, we need the variance of the observed \(x\)-values \[\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(x_{\text{obs}}) &= \text{Var}(x_{\text{true}} + \delta_x) \\ &= \text{Var}(x_{\text{true}}) + \text{Var}(\delta_x) \\ &= \sigma_{\text{range}}^2 + \sigma_x^2. \end{aligned}\] The second line follows because \(x_{\text{true}}\) and \(\delta_x\) are independent, and the variances of independent random variables add.

The Attenuation Factor

An estimator is biased if its average value over many data sets differs from the true value. We therefore compute the average of \(\hat{\gamma}\). For a large sample, the average estimate is the covariance \(\gamma\sigma_{\text{range}}^2\) divided by the variance \(\sigma_{\text{range}}^2 + \sigma_x^2\), so \[ \mathbb{E}[\hat{\gamma}] = \gamma \frac{\sigma_{\text{range}}^2}{\sigma_{\text{range}}^2 + \sigma_x^2} = \gamma \frac{1}{1 + (\sigma_x/\sigma_{\text{range}})^2}. \]This is the main result. The estimate \(\hat{\gamma}\) is related to the true slope \(\gamma\) through an attenuation factor \[ \alpha \equiv \frac{1}{1 + (\sigma_x/\sigma_{\text{range}})^2}. \]

The average slope estimate is therefore \(\alpha\gamma\). The factor \(\alpha\) is below one unless \(\sigma_x = 0\). In Chapters 4 and 5 the inputs were exact, so \(\alpha = 1\) and the slope was unbiased. As \(\sigma_x\) grows, \(\alpha\) falls and the estimated relation weakens. For \(\sigma_x \to \infty\), \(\alpha \to 0\), which is the extreme case above with a horizontal fit. Figure 6.2 shows the fitted slope for two values of \(\sigma_x/\sigma_{\text{range}}\).

The bias depends on the ratio \(\sigma_x/\sigma_{\text{range}}\), which compares the errors with the true spread, as Figure 6.3 shows. When \(\sigma_x\) equals \(\sigma_{\text{range}}\), the observed \(x\)-values have twice the variance of the true values, so their spread is \(\sqrt{2}\) times larger. The covariance stays the same while the variance doubles, so the slope falls to half of its true value, \(\alpha = 1/2\).

Because \(\alpha\) depends only on this ratio and not on the sample size, more data cannot remove the bias of the OLS slope. The \(x\)-errors are random, but they add the variance \(\sigma_x^2\) to the denominator, and averaging over more points does not remove a variance. The \(y\)-errors add only terms to the covariance that average to zero, so \(\alpha\) does not depend on \(\sigma_y\). The bias follows directly from the input uncertainties and affects regressions with uncertain independent variables.

6.4 Practical Implications of Attenuation Bias

To gauge the size of the bias in practice, suppose that the uncertainty in \(x\) is 10% of the spread of the true values. Then \(\sigma_x/\sigma_{\text{range}} = 0.1\) and \(\alpha = 0.99\), a 1% bias in the slope. This may look small, but even a 1% systematic bias can matter. Large samples shrink the random errors to the percent level, so a 1% systematic bias then becomes comparable to them.

In cosmology, for example, photometric redshifts of individual galaxies may have 10% uncertainties. Yet we aim to constrain cosmological parameters, such as the Hubble constant or the dark energy equation of state, to percent-level precision. The same problem appears in many astronomical measurements.

Several examples below give the uncertainty as a fraction of the full range of a sample. The full range is typically several times \(\sigma_{\text{range}}\), so these examples have larger ratios \(\sigma_x/\sigma_{\text{range}}\) and larger biases than the case above.

Stellar age uncertainties are often 1 Gyr or more. Only the few stars with precise ages from asteroseismology, the study of stellar oscillations, do better. An uncertainty of 1 Gyr is at least 7% of the 14 Gyr age of the Universe, the full range of possible ages. Yet we hope to determine the star formation history of galaxies far more precisely from large samples. Relations that depend on age can therefore suffer from attenuation bias.

Careful spectroscopic analyses of chemical abundances typically reach 0.05 to 0.1 dex, where 1 dex is a factor of 10. This is about 10% of the full metallicity range that we observe in our Galaxy. Such an uncertainty can dilute relations that depend on metallicity.

Black hole mass measurements typically carry uncertainties of 0.3 to 0.5 dex. This is about 10% of the 3 to 5 orders of magnitude that black hole masses span. When the mass is the independent variable, the resulting attenuation can bias black hole scaling relations.

Stellar and gas masses typically carry uncertainties of 0.1 to 0.2 dex. When they are the independent variables of scaling relations, such as star formation efficiency against gas mass, attenuation bias can weaken the slopes.

Attenuation bias is a systematic effect that we must correct as we push toward more precise inference. Even a very large sample leaves the 1% bias found above. We therefore need methods that account for uncertainties in both variables.

6.5 Latent Variable Formalism

To account for uncertainties in both variables, we change the likelihood. The new likelihood extends the likelihood of Chapters 4 and 5. There we treated the \(x\)-measurements as fixed, known quantities and modeled only the probability of the \(y\)-values. Now we model the joint probability of \(x\) and \(y\), given their true values and the model parameters.

Recall the model. A true linear relation links the two variables \[ y_{\text{true}} = \gamma x_{\text{true}}. \]The measurements contain errors \[\begin{aligned} x_{\text{obs}} &= x_{\text{true}} + \delta_x \\ y_{\text{obs}} &= y_{\text{true}} + \delta_y \\ &= \gamma x_{\text{true}} + \delta_y. \end{aligned}\]

For the likelihood we also assume that the errors are normal \[\begin{aligned} \delta_x &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_x^2) \\ \delta_y &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_y^2). \end{aligned}\]

Suppose that we know the true value \(x_{\text{true}}\). Then any deviation of \(x_{\text{obs}}\) from \(x_{\text{true}}\) is due to \(\delta_x\) alone, and any deviation of \(y_{\text{obs}}\) from \(\gamma x_{\text{true}}\) is due to \(\delta_y\) alone. Therefore, when we condition on \(x_{\text{true}}\), \(x_{\text{obs}}\) follows a normal distribution centered at \(x_{\text{true}}\) with variance \(\sigma_x^2\). Likewise, \(y_{\text{obs}}\) follows a normal distribution centered at \(\gamma x_{\text{true}}\) with variance \(\sigma_y^2\).

Because the two errors are independent, the joint probability is a product \[ p(x_{\text{obs}}, y_{\text{obs}} \mid x_{\text{true}}, \gamma) = \mathcal{N}(x_{\text{obs}} \mid x_{\text{true}}, \sigma_x^2) \, \mathcal{N}(y_{\text{obs}} \mid \gamma x_{\text{true}}, \sigma_y^2). \]In the case of the M-\(\sigma\) relation, the first factor describes the scatter from the uncertainty in the velocity dispersion. The second describes the scatter from the uncertainty in the black hole mass.

However, we conditioned everything on \(x_{\text{true}}\), and we do not know the true values. If we did, we would be back in the simpler setting of Chapters 4 and 5, with uncertainties only in \(y\). Instead, we treat the unknown true values as extra parameters of the model.

The full likelihood therefore depends on the slope \(\gamma\) and on the true value \(x_{\text{true},i}\) of each observation. We estimate the slope and the true values together. In the M-\(\sigma\) relation these are the slope and the true velocity dispersion of each galaxy. Written out, the likelihood is \[ \mathcal{L}(\gamma, \{x_{\text{true},i}\}) = \prod_{i=1}^N \mathcal{N}(x_{\text{obs},i} \mid x_{\text{true},i}, \sigma_x^2) \, \mathcal{N}(y_{\text{obs},i} \mid \gamma x_{\text{true},i}, \sigma_y^2). \]

At first glance this task looks hard. We added \(N\) new parameters, one \(x_{\text{true},i}\) for each observation. In many problems such additional parameters lead to overfitting (Section 4.7) or to computational difficulties. Here the inference remains possible, because we have \(2N\) measurements for \(N+1\) parameters and we know the sizes of the errors.

Treating the unknown true values as parameters to infer gives a hierarchical structure. At the top is the model parameter \(\gamma\). Below it are the true values \(x_{\text{true},i}\), and at the bottom are the measurements \((x_{\text{obs},i}, y_{\text{obs},i})\).

This hierarchical view is common in astronomy and machine learning. Stellar population studies infer individual stellar parameters together with population-level relations. In cosmology, individual galaxy properties are estimated together with the parameters of large-scale structure.

6.6 Deming Regression

We now solve for both \(x_{\text{true}}\) and \(\gamma\). Recall that the likelihood of all the observations is \[ \mathcal{L}(\gamma, \{x_{\text{true},i}\}) = \prod_{i=1}^N \mathcal{N}(x_{\text{obs},i} \mid x_{\text{true},i}, \sigma_x^2) \, \mathcal{N}(y_{\text{obs},i} \mid \gamma x_{\text{true},i}, \sigma_y^2). \]Expanding the normal distributions gives \[ \mathcal{L}(\gamma, \{x_{\text{true},i}\}) = \prod_{i=1}^N \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma_x^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{(x_{\text{obs},i} - x_{\text{true},i})^2}{2\sigma_x^2}\right) \, \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma_y^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{(y_{\text{obs},i} - \gamma x_{\text{true},i})^2}{2\sigma_y^2}\right). \]Taking the negative logarithm and dropping constant terms gives the negative log-likelihood \[ E(\{x_{\text{true},i}\}, \gamma) = \sum_{i=1}^N \left[\frac{(x_{\text{obs},i} - x_{\text{true},i})^2}{2\sigma_x^2} + \frac{(y_{\text{obs},i} - \gamma x_{\text{true},i})^2}{2\sigma_y^2}\right]. \]The slope \(\gamma\) appears in all terms, but each \(x_{\text{true},i}\) appears only in the \(i\)th term. We can therefore optimize each \(x_{\text{true},i}\) independently for a fixed \(\gamma\), and then use the optimized values to solve for \(\gamma\).

For a single observation \(i\), the negative log-likelihood is \[ E(x_{\text{true},i}, \gamma) = \frac{(x_{\text{obs},i} - x_{\text{true},i})^2}{2\sigma_x^2} + \frac{(y_{\text{obs},i} - \gamma x_{\text{true},i})^2}{2\sigma_y^2}. \]

To find the optimal \(x_{\text{true},i}\), we set the derivative with respect to \(x_{\text{true},i}\) to zero \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial E}{\partial x_{\text{true},i}} &= -\frac{(x_{\text{obs},i} - x_{\text{true},i})}{\sigma_x^2} - \frac{\gamma(y_{\text{obs},i} - \gamma x_{\text{true},i})}{\sigma_y^2} = 0. \end{aligned}\]Rearranging gives \[\begin{aligned} \frac{x_{\text{true},i}}{\sigma_x^2} + \frac{\gamma^2 x_{\text{true},i}}{\sigma_y^2} &= \frac{x_{\text{obs},i}}{\sigma_x^2} + \frac{\gamma y_{\text{obs},i}}{\sigma_y^2} \\ x_{\text{true},i}\left(\frac{1}{\sigma_x^2} + \frac{\gamma^2}{\sigma_y^2}\right) &= \frac{x_{\text{obs},i}}{\sigma_x^2} + \frac{\gamma y_{\text{obs},i}}{\sigma_y^2}. \end{aligned}\]Multiplying both sides by \(\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2\) gives \[\begin{aligned} x_{\text{true},i}(\sigma_y^2 + \gamma^2\sigma_x^2) &= \sigma_y^2x_{\text{obs},i} + \gamma\sigma_x^2y_{\text{obs},i}. \end{aligned}\]

We define the variance ratio \(\lambda = \sigma_y^2/\sigma_x^2\) and divide both sides by \(\sigma_x^2(\lambda + \gamma^2)\), which gives \[ \hat{x}_{\text{true},i} = \frac{\lambda x_{\text{obs},i} + \gamma y_{\text{obs},i}}{\lambda + \gamma^2}. \]With this expression we estimate the true \(x\)-values for a given slope \(\gamma\). We write the estimate with a hat, as for the slope. It combines the observed \(x\)-value, \(x_{\text{obs},i}\), with the value that the \(y\)-measurement predicts, \(y_{\text{obs},i}/\gamma\). We thus use the linear relation between \(x\) and \(y\) to constrain the true values in both dimensions at once. Figure 6.4 shows, for each observation, the shift from \(x_{\text{obs},i}\) to the estimate \(\hat{x}_{\text{true},i}\). For \(\lambda = 1\) the point of the model line at \(\hat{x}_{\text{true},i}\) is the one closest to the observed point, and the method is called orthogonal regression.

With explicit weights, the formula reads \[ \hat{x}_{\text{true},i} = \omega_x x_{\text{obs},i} + \omega_y \frac{y_{\text{obs},i}}{\gamma}, \] where \(\omega_x = \lambda/(\lambda + \gamma^2)\) and \(\omega_y = \gamma^2/(\lambda + \gamma^2)\) are weights that sum to 1. Hence \(\hat{x}_{\text{true},i}\) is a weighted average of \(x_{\text{obs},i}\) and \(y_{\text{obs},i}/\gamma\).

The weights depend on the relative uncertainties. The \(y\)-measurement predicts \(x\) as \(y_{\text{obs},i}/\gamma\), with uncertainty \(\sigma_y/|\gamma|\). If \(\sigma_x\) is small compared with this uncertainty, so that \(\lambda \gg \gamma^2\), the weight \(\omega_x\) approaches 1 and \(\hat{x}_{\text{true},i} \approx x_{\text{obs},i}\), so we trust the \(x\)-measurement. In the opposite limit \(\lambda \ll \gamma^2\), \(\omega_y\) approaches 1 and \(\hat{x}_{\text{true},i} \approx y_{\text{obs},i}/\gamma\), so we infer \(x\) from \(y\). This weighting is what allows Deming regression to correct the attenuation bias. It balances the direct \(x\)-measurements against the constraint of the linear model, so we recover estimates of both the slope and the true values.

6.7 Analytical Solution

To find \(\gamma\), we return to the negative log-likelihood. The estimates \(\hat{x}_{\text{true},i}\) depend on \(\gamma\), so we substitute them below. \[ E(\{x_{\text{true},i}\}, \gamma) = \sum_{i=1}^N \left[\frac{(x_{\text{obs},i} - x_{\text{true},i})^2}{2\sigma_x^2} + \frac{(y_{\text{obs},i} - \gamma x_{\text{true},i})^2}{2\sigma_y^2}\right]. \]Setting the derivative with respect to \(\gamma\) to zero at the estimates \(\hat{x}_{\text{true},i}\) gives \[ \frac{\partial E}{\partial \gamma} = -\sum_{i=1}^N \frac{x_{\text{true},i}(y_{\text{obs},i} - \gamma x_{\text{true},i})}{\sigma_y^2} = 0. \]

Because the derivative with respect to each \(x_{\text{true},i}\) vanishes at the estimates, the chain rule makes this the derivative of the optimized negative log-likelihood. The expression for \(\hat{x}_{\text{true},i}\) also gives the second factor of each term \[\begin{aligned} y_{\text{obs},i} - \gamma\hat{x}_{\text{true},i} &= y_{\text{obs},i} - \frac{\gamma(\lambda x_{\text{obs},i} + \gamma y_{\text{obs},i})}{\lambda + \gamma^2} \\ &= \frac{(\lambda + \gamma^2)y_{\text{obs},i} - \gamma(\lambda x_{\text{obs},i} + \gamma y_{\text{obs},i})}{\lambda + \gamma^2} \\ &= \frac{\lambda(y_{\text{obs},i} - \gamma x_{\text{obs},i})}{\lambda + \gamma^2}. \end{aligned}\] Substituting both expressions, the condition becomes \[ -\sum_{i=1}^N \frac{1}{\sigma_y^2} \left(\frac{\lambda x_{\text{obs},i} + \gamma y_{\text{obs},i}}{\lambda + \gamma^2}\right)\left(\frac{\lambda(y_{\text{obs},i} - \gamma x_{\text{obs},i})}{\lambda + \gamma^2}\right) = 0. \]Dividing by the factor \(-\lambda/[\sigma_y^2(\lambda + \gamma^2)^2]\), which does not depend on \(i\), gives \[ \sum_{i=1}^N (\lambda x_{\text{obs},i} + \gamma y_{\text{obs},i})(y_{\text{obs},i} - \gamma x_{\text{obs},i}) = 0. \]Expanding the products gives \[ \sum_{i=1}^N [\lambda x_{\text{obs},i}y_{\text{obs},i} - \lambda\gamma x_{\text{obs},i}^2 + \gamma y_{\text{obs},i}^2 - \gamma^2 x_{\text{obs},i}y_{\text{obs},i}] = 0. \]

As in Chapter 3, we describe the data by summary statistics, here the sums of squares and cross products. Here \(\mathbb{E}\) is the sample mean, and the sums are defined by \[\begin{aligned} S_{xx} &= \sum_{i=1}^N (x_{\text{obs},i} - \mathbb{E}[x_{\text{obs}}])^2 \\ S_{yy} &= \sum_{i=1}^N (y_{\text{obs},i} - \mathbb{E}[y_{\text{obs}}])^2 \\ S_{xy} &= \sum_{i=1}^N (x_{\text{obs},i} - \mathbb{E}[x_{\text{obs}}])(y_{\text{obs},i} - \mathbb{E}[y_{\text{obs}}]). \end{aligned}\]These sums differ from the sample variance and covariance only by a factor of \(N\) \[\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(x_{\text{obs}}) &= \frac{1}{N}S_{xx} \\ \text{Var}(y_{\text{obs}}) &= \frac{1}{N}S_{yy} \\ \text{Cov}(x_{\text{obs}},y_{\text{obs}}) &= \frac{1}{N}S_{xy}. \end{aligned}\]For centered variables, where \(\mathbb{E}[x_{\text{obs}}] = \mathbb{E}[y_{\text{obs}}] = 0\), they simplify to \[\begin{aligned} S_{xx} &= \sum_{i=1}^N x_{\text{obs},i}^2 \\ S_{yy} &= \sum_{i=1}^N y_{\text{obs},i}^2 \\ S_{xy} &= \sum_{i=1}^N x_{\text{obs},i}y_{\text{obs},i}. \end{aligned}\]

The Deming Estimator

With these statistics, the equation takes the compact form \[ \lambda S_{xy} - \lambda\gamma S_{xx} + \gamma S_{yy} - \gamma^2 S_{xy} = 0. \]Rearranging into standard quadratic form gives \[ \gamma^2 S_{xy} - \gamma(S_{yy} - \lambda S_{xx}) - \lambda S_{xy} = 0. \]This is a quadratic equation of the form \(a\gamma^2 + b\gamma + c = 0\), with solutions \(\gamma = (-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac})/(2a)\). Here \(a = S_{xy}\), \(b = -(S_{yy} - \lambda S_{xx})\) and \(c = -\lambda S_{xy}\). The solution is the Deming regression estimator, again written \(\hat{\gamma}\), with one root for each sign \[ \hat{\gamma} = \frac{S_{yy} - \lambda S_{xx} \pm \sqrt{(S_{yy} - \lambda S_{xx})^2 + 4\lambda S_{xy}^2}}{2S_{xy}}. \]

The two roots have opposite signs, because their product is \(-\lambda\). The maximum likelihood estimate is the root that minimizes the negative log-likelihood. Once the \(x_{\text{true},i}\) are optimized, the negative log-likelihood tends to the same constant as \(\gamma \to \pm\infty\), because \(\hat{x}_{\text{true},i}\) goes to zero while \(\gamma\hat{x}_{\text{true},i}\) goes to \(y_{\text{obs},i}\). Its derivative, the condition above, vanishes only at the two roots, so one is a minimum and the other a maximum.

At \(\gamma = 0\), between the roots, the derivative is \(-S_{xy}/\sigma_y^2\), so the function falls toward the root with the sign of \(S_{xy}\), which is the minimum. The root with the plus sign has this sign, because the square root exceeds \(|S_{yy} - \lambda S_{xx}|\). We take this root. The plus root also gives the correct limit for \(\sigma_x \to 0\), where we recover the OLS slope, as we show below.

We obtain a direct solution without iteration, although both the true values \(x_{\text{true},i}\) and the slope \(\gamma\) are unknown. The reason is that the problem splits into two steps.

Recall from Section 4.4 that a convex function opens upward and has a single lowest point. The negative log-likelihood is not convex in all the variables jointly. For any fixed \(\gamma\), however, it is quadratic, and hence convex, in each \(x_{\text{true},i}\), so its optimal values \(\hat{x}_{\text{true},i}\) have a closed form. It is also convex in \(\gamma\) for fixed \(x_{\text{true},i}\). Substituting the optimal \(\hat{x}_{\text{true},i}\) back reduces the problem to one dimension, the quadratic in \(\gamma\).

Recovering the OLS Slope

Figure 6.5 compares OLS and Deming regression on simulated data. We now check analytically that the Deming estimate \(\hat{\gamma}\) reduces to the OLS slope, also written \(\hat{\gamma}\), when \(\sigma_x \to 0\), or equivalently when \(\lambda = \sigma_y^2/\sigma_x^2 \to \infty\).

First we note that \[ S_{yy} - \lambda S_{xx} = \lambda\left(\frac{S_{yy}}{\lambda} - S_{xx}\right). \]The square root can be rewritten as \[ \sqrt{(S_{yy} - \lambda S_{xx})^2 + 4\lambda S_{xy}^2} = \sqrt{\lambda^2\left(\frac{S_{yy}}{\lambda} - S_{xx}\right)^2 + 4\lambda S_{xy}^2}. \]Factoring \(\lambda\) out of the square root gives \[ \sqrt{(S_{yy} - \lambda S_{xx})^2 + 4\lambda S_{xy}^2} = \lambda \sqrt{\left(\frac{S_{yy}}{\lambda} - S_{xx}\right)^2 + \frac{4S_{xy}^2}{\lambda}}. \]This allows us to write the estimator as \[ \hat{\gamma} = \frac{S_{yy} - \lambda S_{xx} + \sqrt{(S_{yy} - \lambda S_{xx})^2 + 4\lambda S_{xy}^2}}{2S_{xy}} \] \[ \hat{\gamma} = \frac{\lambda\left(\frac{S_{yy}}{\lambda} - S_{xx} + \sqrt{\left(\frac{S_{yy}}{\lambda} - S_{xx}\right)^2 + \frac{4S_{xy}^2}{\lambda}}\right)}{2S_{xy}}. \]

For large \(\lambda\), we expand the square root with the approximation \[ \sqrt{1+\epsilon} \approx 1+\frac{\epsilon}{2}, \] where \(\epsilon\) is small. We write the term under the square root as \[ \left(S_{xx} - \frac{S_{yy}}{\lambda}\right)^2 + \frac{4S_{xy}^2}{\lambda} = S_{xx}^2\left(1 + \left(-\frac{2S_{yy}}{\lambda S_{xx}} + \frac{S_{yy}^2}{\lambda^2 S_{xx}^2} + \frac{4S_{xy}^2}{\lambda S_{xx}^2}\right)\right). \]

As \(\lambda \to \infty\), the term \(S_{yy}^2/(\lambda^2 S_{xx}^2)\) is of second order in \(1/\lambda\), and we drop it. The other two terms are of first order. We keep them, because the leading terms cancel below and the factor \(\lambda\) lifts them to order one. Then \[ \epsilon = -\frac{2S_{yy}}{\lambda S_{xx}} + \frac{S_{yy}^2}{\lambda^2 S_{xx}^2} + \frac{4S_{xy}^2}{\lambda S_{xx}^2} \approx -\frac{2S_{yy}}{\lambda S_{xx}} + \frac{4S_{xy}^2}{\lambda S_{xx}^2}, \] which becomes small as \(\lambda\) grows. This gives \[ \sqrt{\left(S_{xx} - \frac{S_{yy}}{\lambda}\right)^2 + \frac{4S_{xy}^2}{\lambda}} \approx S_{xx} - \frac{S_{yy}}{\lambda} + \frac{2S_{xy}^2}{\lambda S_{xx}}. \]

Substituting back gives \[ \hat{\gamma} = \frac{\lambda\left[-S_{xx} + \frac{S_{yy}}{\lambda} + \left(S_{xx} - \frac{S_{yy}}{\lambda} + \frac{2S_{xy}^2}{\lambda S_{xx}}\right)\right]}{2S_{xy}}. \]The \(S_{xx}\) terms and the \(S_{yy}/\lambda\) terms cancel, which leaves \[ \hat{\gamma} = \frac{\lambda\left(\frac{2S_{xy}^2}{\lambda S_{xx}}\right)}{2S_{xy}} = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}} = \frac{\text{Cov}(x_{\text{obs}},y_{\text{obs}})}{\text{Var}(x_{\text{obs}})}. \]In the limit \(\lambda \to \infty\), which is \(\sigma_x \to 0\), the Deming slope therefore converges to the OLS slope \(S_{xy}/S_{xx}\). This is the maximum likelihood estimator that we derived for uncertainty in \(y\) only.

6.8 Extension to Heteroscedastic Uncertainties

So far we assumed homogeneous uncertainties, so that \(\sigma_x\) and \(\sigma_y\) are constant across the observations. This simplification gave us intuition and analytical results. Real astronomical measurements often have uncertainties that differ by large factors from point to point within one data set. In the M-\(\sigma\) relation, for example, the velocity dispersions may be more precise for brighter galaxies. Nearby galaxies also typically have more precise measurements than distant ones. The black hole mass uncertainties may depend on the measurement technique.

The same pattern appears in many other astronomical contexts. Brighter objects generally have more precise measurements than fainter ones, and different measurement techniques often have different uncertainties.

For heteroscedastic uncertainties, where \(\sigma_{x,i}\) and \(\sigma_{y,i}\) vary with \(i\), the derivation follows the same steps. We start from the likelihood, but now each data point has its own uncertainties \[ \mathcal{L}(\gamma, \{x_{\text{true},i}\}) = \prod_{i=1}^N \mathcal{N}(x_{\text{obs},i} \mid x_{\text{true},i}, \sigma_{x,i}^2) \, \mathcal{N}(y_{\text{obs},i} \mid \gamma x_{\text{true},i}, \sigma_{y,i}^2). \]Taking the negative logarithm and dropping constant terms gives the negative log-likelihood \[ E(\{x_{\text{true},i}\}, \gamma) = \sum_{i=1}^N \left[\frac{(x_{\text{obs},i} - x_{\text{true},i})^2}{2\sigma_{x,i}^2} + \frac{(y_{\text{obs},i} - \gamma x_{\text{true},i})^2}{2\sigma_{y,i}^2}\right]. \]

As before, we first solve for each \(x_{\text{true},i}\) by setting the derivative with respect to \(x_{\text{true},i}\) to zero \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial E}{\partial x_{\text{true},i}} &= -\frac{(x_{\text{obs},i} - x_{\text{true},i})}{\sigma_{x,i}^2} - \frac{\gamma(y_{\text{obs},i} - \gamma x_{\text{true},i})}{\sigma_{y,i}^2} = 0. \end{aligned}\]Rearranging gives \[\begin{aligned} \frac{x_{\text{true},i}}{\sigma_{x,i}^2} + \frac{\gamma^2 x_{\text{true},i}}{\sigma_{y,i}^2} &= \frac{x_{\text{obs},i}}{\sigma_{x,i}^2} + \frac{\gamma y_{\text{obs},i}}{\sigma_{y,i}^2} \\ x_{\text{true},i}\left(\frac{1}{\sigma_{x,i}^2} + \frac{\gamma^2}{\sigma_{y,i}^2}\right) &= \frac{x_{\text{obs},i}}{\sigma_{x,i}^2} + \frac{\gamma y_{\text{obs},i}}{\sigma_{y,i}^2}. \end{aligned}\]Solving for \(x_{\text{true},i}\) gives \[ \hat{x}_{\text{true},i} = \frac{\sigma_{y,i}^2 x_{\text{obs},i} + \gamma \sigma_{x,i}^2 y_{\text{obs},i}}{\sigma_{y,i}^2 + \gamma^2 \sigma_{x,i}^2}. \]This expression is analogous to the homoscedastic result, but the weights now depend on the individual uncertainties \(\sigma_{x,i}\) and \(\sigma_{y,i}\). It is a weighted average of the direct measurement \(x_{\text{obs},i}\), with weight \(\sigma_{y,i}^2\), and the model-inferred value \(y_{\text{obs},i}/\gamma\), with weight \(\gamma^2\sigma_{x,i}^2\). When a point has a large uncertainty in one dimension, the estimate relies more on the other dimension.

Setting the derivative with respect to \(\gamma\) to zero gives \[ \frac{\partial E}{\partial \gamma} = -\sum_{i=1}^N \frac{x_{\text{true},i}(y_{\text{obs},i} - \gamma x_{\text{true},i})}{\sigma_{y,i}^2} = 0. \]Here \(y_{\text{obs},i} - \gamma\hat{x}_{\text{true},i} = \sigma_{y,i}^2(y_{\text{obs},i} - \gamma x_{\text{obs},i})/(\sigma_{y,i}^2 + \gamma^2\sigma_{x,i}^2)\), which follows as in the homoscedastic case. Substituting both expressions, the condition becomes \[ -\sum_{i=1}^N \frac{1}{\sigma_{y,i}^2} \left(\frac{\sigma_{y,i}^2 x_{\text{obs},i} + \gamma \sigma_{x,i}^2 y_{\text{obs},i}}{\sigma_{y,i}^2 + \gamma^2 \sigma_{x,i}^2}\right)\left(\frac{\sigma_{y,i}^2(y_{\text{obs},i} - \gamma x_{\text{obs},i})}{\sigma_{y,i}^2 + \gamma^2 \sigma_{x,i}^2}\right) = 0. \]

The factor \(\sigma_{y,i}^2\) cancels the weight \(1/\sigma_{y,i}^2\), which gives the function \(F(\gamma)\) whose zero we need \[ F(\gamma) = \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{(\sigma_{y,i}^2 x_{\text{obs},i} + \gamma \sigma_{x,i}^2 y_{\text{obs},i})(y_{\text{obs},i} - \gamma x_{\text{obs},i})}{(\sigma_{y,i}^2 + \gamma^2 \sigma_{x,i}^2)^2} = 0. \]Unlike the quadratic equation of the homoscedastic case, the equation \(F(\gamma) = 0\) has no closed-form solution in general. Each term has a weight that depends on \(\gamma\) and on its own uncertainties. We therefore solve it numerically.

As in the homoscedastic case, \(F\) is minus the derivative of the negative log-likelihood after the \(x_{\text{true},i}\) are optimized. The estimate \(\hat{\gamma}\) is therefore the zero where \(F\) changes from positive to negative, and there the negative log-likelihood is a minimum.

Grid Search

The simplest approach evaluates \(F(\gamma)\) on a grid of \(\gamma\)-values and finds where it crosses zero. This is computationally inefficient, but reliable and easy to implement. Figure 6.6(b) shows \(F(\gamma)\) evaluated on such a grid.

Newton’s Method

Newton’s method replaces \(F(\gamma)\) by its tangent line at the current guess \(\gamma_n\) and moves to where that line crosses zero. Repeating this step approaches the root through the iteration \[ \gamma_{n+1} = \gamma_n - \frac{F(\gamma_n)}{F'(\gamma_n)}. \] Near the root, one step roughly doubles the number of correct digits, which is called quadratic convergence. However, the method needs the derivative \(F'(\gamma)\).

Library Root Finders

Standard numerical libraries offer reliable root finders, such as Brent’s method. It keeps an interval around the root and shrinks it by bisection, secant steps and inverse quadratic interpolation. The starting interval must have opposite signs of \(F\) at its two ends, so a root lies inside. Such root finders converge well without derivatives.

Like the homoscedastic solution, the heteroscedastic solution corrects attenuation bias, but the correction is now specific to each data point and its uncertainties. Points with smaller uncertainties carry more weight in determining \(\gamma\), so we use all the data while the most precise measurements dominate the inference. When all \(\sigma_{x,i} \to 0\), we recover the weighted least squares solution of Chapter 4, as in the homoscedastic limit above.

This ends our study of linear regression. Many astronomical problems have a discrete label as the output instead, such as star or galaxy. Chapter 7 treats these classification problems.

6.9 Tutorial: Fitting the Tully-Fisher Relation

This tutorial applies the attenuation factor and Deming regression of this chapter to the Tully-Fisher relation. It links the rotation velocity of a galaxy to its baryonic mass, the mass of stars and gas. Its slope matters for galaxy formation and for distances. The full tutorial can be found at https://statml.org/ as tutorial 6.

A galaxy with more baryons rotates faster, because it sits in a more massive halo of dark matter, whose gravity sets the rotation speed. In nearby disk galaxies, we measure the rotation velocity from spectra and the baryonic mass from the radiation of stars and gas. On logarithmic axes the two lie close to a straight line (Figure 6.7a). Its slope links the stars and gas to the halo, and so constrains how galaxies assemble their baryons. The relation also gives distances, because the rotation velocity predicts how much light a galaxy emits.

Both uses depend on the slope, so the fit matters. In Chapters 4 and 5 the inputs were exact and the errors were in the output. Here the rotation velocity, our input, carries errors, for example from the tilt of the disk. Ordinary least squares (OLS) treats the input as exact. Errors in the velocity, which spread the points sideways, then flatten the OLS slope by the attenuation factor (Section 6.3).

To account for this, Deming regression allows errors in both variables, so it uses the errors in the velocity that OLS ignores. As in Section 6.5, it treats the true velocity of each galaxy as a latent variable and infers it together with the slope. The errors differ from galaxy to galaxy, so the fit uses the heteroscedastic form of Section 6.8.

The tutorial compares the two fits for real galaxies. It adds a systematic uncertainty to the velocity errors, so that they match the scatter of the galaxies. In Figure 6.7a the Deming line is steeper than the OLS line, the direction that the flattening of OLS leads us to expect. To judge whether the gap is real, the bootstrap of Section 3.7 gives the sampling noise of each slope (Figure 6.7b). The gap between the two slopes is larger than the noise of either slope.

Noise in the input flattens an OLS fit, and Deming regression allows for that noise. The bootstrap shows whether the difference is larger than the sampling noise. Many scaling relations in astronomy have uncertain inputs. When the input error is not negligible, ignoring it biases the slope, and a biased slope changes the physical conclusions drawn from the relation.

Further Reading

Adcock (1878) developed what is now called orthogonal regression. Pearson (1901) found the lines of closest fit when both variables contain errors. Deming (1943) popularized the weighted least squares fit for a known ratio of error variances that now carries his name. Golub and Van Loan (1980) analyzed total least squares, a fit with errors in both variables, with the singular value decomposition. Van Huffel and Vandewalle (1991) treat its computation and sensitivity. Fuller (1987) covers the theory of measurement error models. Carroll et al. (2006) extend these methods to nonlinear models. Isobe et al. (1990) compared regression methods for astronomical data. Akritas and Bershady (1996) developed an estimator for errors in both variables, with correlated and unequal uncertainties and intrinsic scatter. Kelly (2007) developed Bayesian methods for heteroscedastic errors, intrinsic scatter and selection effects. Bentler and Weeks (1980) developed a general model of linear relations among latent variables. Carroll and Ruppert (1996) examined the use and misuse of orthogonal regression, which typically overestimates the slope when intrinsic scatter is ignored. Ting (2025, 2026) discussed attenuation bias in the context of astronomy and how to correct it in neural networks. Lelli et al. (2016) published SPARC, the sample of nearby disk galaxies with Spitzer infrared photometry and accurate rotation curves. This tutorial takes its galaxies from it.
